lines.text: A fly's wings, then a splash.
lines.phonemes: ɐ flˈaɪz wˈɪŋz, ðˈɛn ɐ splˈæʃ.

lines.text: First, a fly. A housefly beats its wings about two hundred times a second. Slow it a hundred times, and that's two beats a second. A mosquito's wings beat about five hundred times a second. Here, that's five beats a second. You can count them on one hand. Now look at the tap. A drop of water swells there, heavier and heavier, until it lets go. It falls into the cup. It hits, and the water climbs into a crown. The whole crown forms in a few hundredths of a second. At this speed, that takes a few seconds. You can watch each point of the crown rise. Then little drops pinch off, and fly outward. The cup rings. The water settles, and the surface goes flat again. The cup sits still while all this happens. Nothing else in the kitchen has moved yet. Nothing here moved faster than you could follow, once you gave it time. But the next thing happens faster than a splash, in a hot pan on the stove.
